Shake this device to open a guide for the current screen.
All guides

Overview
Get started
Limits and safety
Read documentation
This device has no accelerometer.
Start the server
Shevery lets approved apps use system APIs through a server started with ADB or root.
Open Home and choose root, wireless debugging, or USB debugging from a computer or OTG device. Use the exact command shown on Home for USB.
On non-rooted devices, you may need to start the server again after reboot unless you have configured autostart.
Wireless debugging
Start Shevery over ADB without a computer on Android 11 or later.
Connect to Wi-Fi, enable Wireless debugging in Developer options, and open the pairing tutorial from Home. Pair using the port and code shown in Android, then tap Start in Shevery.
The pairing port can differ from the connection port. Keep the device awake and approve pairing only on a trusted network.
Comput terminal
Run shell commands through the active Shevery server and view output as it arrives.
Start the server, then open Terminal. Enter a command or choose a preset. Use macros to save and replay a sequence.
Commands use the server’s ADB or root privileges. Review commands and macros before running them. ADB mode strips familiar host prefixes, while host-only operations still require a computer.
Commandium AI
Generate a shell command from a description or ask for an explanation of a failed command.
Open Settings → AI → AI provider. Add an OpenAI-compatible provider, choose a model, and select the provider as active. Open Commandium from Comput.
Your provider receives prompts and any command output you send for explanations. Keep secrets out of prompts and use ReCommand to review generated commands before running them.
ADB modules
Install modules that can run scripts and, depending on policy, provide a WebUI or background service.
Open ADB Modules and select a ZIP with module.prop at the archive root, or install from the catalog. Open the installed module to see its available actions.
Review the source before running a module. Scripts use the server’s privileges. Keep the default SAFE policy unless a module needs additional access.
Module catalog
Find modules published on GitHub with the shevery-modules topic.
Open Catalog from ADB Modules. Inspect a module before installing. Choose source files or release ZIPs in the module update settings.
GitHub rate limits anonymous searches. An optional personal access token raises the limit. Keep the token private and install only from authors you trust.
App and module updates
Shevery checks GitHub releases for app updates and checks each module’s configured update source.
In Settings → Updates, choose Stable or Beta and a check frequency, or check manually. Review available module updates in ADB Modules.
Beta includes pre-releases. Android asks you to confirm app installation. Review module releases before applying updates.
Device Owner and Dhizuku
Device Owner settings show ownership and delegation. Experimental Dhizuku mode bridges Shevery to a device owner managed by Dhizuku.
Start Shevery via USB/OTG or wireless debugging first, then start Dhizuku. Enable Dhizuku mode under Settings → Application. Use Device Owner settings to inspect delegation or transfer options.
Owner and delegated privileges affect device-wide policy. Confirm the receiving app and the privileges before granting or transferring access.
Security and authentication
Protect access to Shevery and sensitive actions with biometrics or the device credential.
Open Settings → Security. Enable authentication, choose a session timeout, and select the actions that should require confirmation.
When a protected session expires in the background, Shevery locks on return and drops temporary grants from that session.
Compatibility stubs
Bridge legacy apps that expect the official Shizuku or Dhizuku package to the Shevery service.
Open Settings → Application → Compatibility Stubs. Choose the bridge required by the app and confirm installation. Open the legacy app and authorize access when prompted.
The bridge uses the original package ID. Android cannot install it alongside the original app with that same ID.
Hide Developer options
Temporarily turns off the device-wide Developer options setting while a selected app is in the foreground.
Open the feature, grant Usage access, and start Shevery through Shizuku or configure it as Device Owner. Select the apps that should trigger the change.
The setting affects the whole device while it is off. If Shevery is force-stopped, reopen it so Android can let it restore the setting.
Hide USB debugging
Temporarily turns off USB debugging while a selected app is in the foreground.
Grant Usage access, then start Shevery through Shizuku or configure it as Device Owner. Enable the switch next to each app that should trigger the change.
This changes USB debugging device-wide and can interrupt ADB connections. If you force-stop Shevery, reopen it to allow cleanup.
Network firewall
Block an app’s network access on Android 11 or later using Android’s firewall.
Start Shevery with Shizuku, open Firewall, and switch on blocking for the chosen app. Turn the switch off to remove the rule Shevery added.
The firewall chain is shared. Enabling it can activate rules from other apps and blocking a package can affect others sharing its Android user ID.
Shevery Connectors
Allow third-party activators to get the server start command and enable incoming automation actions.
Open Settings → Automation and enable Shevery Connectors. Check the connector status and automation fields from Home → View intents.
Connectors are off by default. Direct actions require a secret token. Keep it private and turn off Connectors when you no longer need external control.
App authorization
Choose which apps can use the elevated Shevery API.
Start the server. When an app asks for access, check which app made the request and decide whether to allow it. Review and revoke grants from Authorized apps.
Grant access only to apps you trust. Revoking access affects later API calls. It cannot undo changes an app already made.
Tasker and MacroDroid
Automate starting, stopping, restarting, or toggling the Shevery server.
Enable Connectors in Settings → Automation. In Tasker, add a Shevery Tasker plugin action. In MacroDroid, use a broadcast and copy the action, receiver, and token from Automation.
An automation setup still needs a supported start method. Update saved direct actions whenever you regenerate the auth token.
Automation intents
The public broadcasts let an automation app control the Shevery server.
Enable Connectors. Copy the action, target package, receiver, and auth token from Settings → Automation or Home → View intents.
Use the documented public actions. Keep the auth token private. Regenerating it invalidates existing direct broadcasts.
Settings
Configure startup, appearance, security, automation, and other Shevery options.
Open the relevant section from the Settings hub. Use Application for startup behavior, Appearance for interface preferences, and Backups to export or restore a ZIP.
Keep backup archives private because they can contain preferences, app authorizations, and modules.
Module access policy
Control which actions, background tasks, and WebUI capabilities a module can use.
Open Settings → Modules and keep SAFE for routine use. Choose CUSTOM if a module needs a specific permission. Review its scripts before marking it trusted.
Trust bypasses several restrictions. Allow background actions only if required and keep ReCommand enabled for an extra review before executing scripts.
Troubleshooting
Find answers for installation, wireless pairing, server stoppages, and module errors.
Check the port and pairing code if wireless pairing fails. If the server keeps stopping, check battery settings and the ErrorProtect watchdog. For module errors, review the installer output.
For a bug report, include the device model, Android version, start method, and relevant logs. Remove tokens, API keys, and personal information before sharing logs.
How Shevery works
Shevery runs a privileged server and lets approved apps reach system APIs through Binder IPC.
Start the server and grant access to an app you trust. The app can then use the Shevery API for supported operations.
Available permissions depend on the server’s identity and Android version. An ADB-started server runs with shell privileges.
Publish a module
A GitHub repository can make a module discoverable in the Shevery catalog.
Put module.prop at the repository root, add the shevery-modules topic, and publish a ZIP release if you support release installs.
Keep the module ID stable and increase versionCode for each update. Give users a way to review your scripts before installation.
Build from source
Build the Shevery manager and its native components from the project repository.
Clone the repository with submodules. Install the Android SDK and NDK required by the selected revision, then run the included Gradle wrapper.
Check the build configuration of your checkout for tool versions. Android requires a matching signing key to install over an existing copy.
